E063-01.notes: Original is a comma splice (two independent clauses). C is a fused sentence; D inserts a comma after 'and' that breaks the clause join. Only B, with a period, works. Facts check out: 1858 competition, Greensward Plan, swamps and rocky outcrops.

E063-02.notes: B, C and D are all truly redundant ('a lot of very many', 'many thousands ... numerous', 'many thousands ... in large numbers'). 'Many thousands' understates the actual number (about 270,000 trees and shrubs) but is accurate.

E063-03.notes: The sentence contrasts how the park looks (natural) with the fact that it was designed, so a concessive word is needed. 'Because' and 'Since' give a false cause; 'Unless' sets up a nonsense condition.

flags.note: There is no NO CHANGE option, yet choice D repeats the original text exactly while the stem is the standard 'best for the underlined portion' wording. Real ACT items with an underline always offer NO CHANGE as A. Recommend making A 'NO CHANGE' and reordering the choices.

E063-04.notes: A gives 'roads below for crosstown traffic below the level', which says 'below' twice and misplaces the modifier. B ('tucked also roads') has awkward word order. C uses commas to split the verb from its object ('tucked, for crosstown traffic, roads below'); it is grammatical but awkward and clearly worse than D. D is the original wording and is clear.

E063-05.notes: Adding the sentence is relevant: it names the roads just described (transverse roads) and says they are still in use, which is accurate (the 65th, 79th, 86th and 97th Street transverses). B fails because sentence 5 gives neither the name nor current use, so this is not mere repetition. A is wrong because the sentence is not about traffic laws. D is wrong because it does not explain the competition result.

E063-06.notes: This needs a plain plural with no noun owned. A and B are possessives. C is singular, which clashes with 'a community of mostly ... homeowners'. Factual claim is fine: the village was mostly African American and included many property owners.

E063-07.notes: A puts a comma between the compound subject and its verb. C puts a comma after 'and'. D misplaces commas in two spots. B is the standard series punctuation. Churches, homes and a school matches the historical record.

E063-08.notes: 'Today' requires the present tense. B, C and D are past, past perfect and future perfect.

E063-09.notes: Only A mentions Seneca Village, so only A ties the present back to the cost in the third paragraph. B, C and D are unrelated facts (D's 'more than 800 acres' is accurate, about 843 acres).

E063-10.notes: A is false (no tree-by-tree detail). C is false (the transverse roads get only one sentence). D is false (sentence 4 says almost every hill and pond was designed). Calling the design coverage 'brief' is arguable, since design gets two short paragraphs, but the essay never explains how the natural look was achieved and spends its second half on Seneca Village, so B is clearly best.

E063-11.notes: A's semicolon is followed by a fragment. B, with no comma, invites 'Sea remarkably well preserved'. C's 'and' leaves the phrase nothing parallel to join. D sets off a closing descriptive phrase about the wreck, which is standard. Facts check out: the wreck was found in 2022 at about 3,008 m, roughly 9,870 ft, so 'nearly 10,000 feet' is accurate.

E063-12.notes: The essay is about survival and rescue. A is false (it never explains how pack ice forms). B: finding the wreck in 2022 was not a discovery made during the expedition, and it is a one-sentence coda. D is false (the essay names Antarctica and the Weddell Sea). Dates, crew counts, the roughly 800-mile boat trip and the four rescue attempts are all accurate. 'Not one member of the crew' is fine because it refers to the Endurance (Weddell Sea) party.

E063-13.notes: A, B and D are redundant ('steadily and continuously at a constant rate', 'steadily and at a steady pace', 'continuously, without ever stopping'). With C, 'dripped oil steadily into an engine while it ran' is complete. Facts check out: born 1844 in Ontario, parents had escaped slavery in Kentucky, trained in Scotland, worked for Michigan Central, 1872 lubricator patent, 50+ patents, ironing board and lawn sprinkler, disputed 'real McCoy' origin.
